clue.text: Arguing with dad, getting into spirits, teenage trouble

indicators.note: Anything that gets into a drink ends up surrounded by it, so the letters named before this land inside the drink that follows.

parts.note: gin is a spirit, and these four letters open up after the first
to row with someone is to argue with them
pa = dad, the crossword's standard short father

explanation.surface: A family row with dad while the drink flows, and the teenager at the centre of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spirits' wants to be mood — the sulks an adolescent gets into — and it is the drinks cabinet instead.
explanation.definitionFit: teenage trouble -> GROWING PAINS: the aches and awkwardness of adolescence, and by extension the early troubles of anything young.

clue.text: Text read by minister, my suggestion for vin rosé

indicators.note: The setter is proposing a treatment of the words that follow, and the treatment proposed is a rewrite, which the first half of the answer then names.

parts.note: the treatment being proposed, written out in full: to revise is to work something over again
the seven letters of VIN ROSE resettle into a new order

explanation.surface: The lesson a minister reads out, beside the speaker's own recommendation about pink wine.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer describes what has been done to the wine: it is a revised version of those seven letters. The Revised Version is the 1885 English Bible, which is what gets read from a pulpit.
explanation.definitionFit: Text read by minister -> REVISED VERSION: the Revised Version is a nineteenth-century English Bible, so it is literally a text read aloud in church.

clue.text: Cop caught by reduction in force is hopeful

indicators.note: To be caught by something is to be held inside it, so the first word ends up within the word that catches it.

parts.note: to wane is to dwindle in strength, and these four letters part after the third
to cop someone is to nab them, both meaning to catch

explanation.surface: A police officer let go in a round of layoffs, still optimistic about work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cop' reads as the noun, a policeman, and is the verb — to cop is to seize. 'Reduction in force' is a redundancy notice on the surface and plain dwindling in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: hopeful -> WANNABE: a hopeful is someone angling for a role they have not got yet, which is exactly what a wannabe is.

clue.text: See blonde misapplied red running down face?

indicators.note: Make-up put on wrongly goes where it should not, so the letters it describes end up out of their proper places.

parts.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

explanation.surface: Hair dye or lipstick put on badly, leaving colour streaked down someone's face.
explanation.walkthrough: The picture is botched cosmetics, so the red reads as make-up rather than blood, and 'misapplied' looks like a comment on the girl instead of an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: red running down face -> NOSEBLEED: not a synonym but a description of what one looks like, the setter defining by the picture it makes.

clue.text: Charity supports US criminal upset with charges met earlier

indicators.note: Upset means tipped over, and letters tipped over in a down entry come back up in the opposite order.
A support sits underneath whatever it holds up, so in a down entry the charity's letters take the bottom cells.

parts.note: American police slang for the perpetrator of a crime is a perp, here written the other way round
charity is aid, relief given to those who need it

explanation.surface: A charity standing behind an American crook who is aggrieved about the charges brought against him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' looks like the criminal's mood and is the instruction to turn his letters round, while 'charges' plays on criminal charges rather than fees.
explanation.definitionFit: with charges met earlier -> PREPAID: a prepaid item is one whose cost has already been settled before it is used or sent.

clue.text: Winning score one put up for seed playing

indicators.note: The letter that stands for one is I, and putting it up in a down entry lifts it to the front of the letters it was sitting among.

parts.note: a seed is a pip, and with its I lifted to the front the three letters read in this order
a match or a show that is on is playing

explanation.surface: A scoreline from a match: a point put up while the seeded player was on.
explanation.walkthrough: In judo an ippon ends the contest outright, so 'winning score' is exact rather than loose. Nothing is shuffled here — only the I climbs, and the two Ps stay put.
explanation.definitionFit: Winning score -> IPPON: judo's full point, awarded for a clean throw and enough on its own to win the bout.

clue.text: American feeds permanently dirty bear

indicators.note: Something fed into a machine passes inside it, so the American letters are swallowed by the words that follow.

parts.note: to stain is to dirty something so the mark stays, and these five letters open after the first
US = American, the standard two-letter shorthand

explanation.surface: Someone from the States putting food out for a bear that never washes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bear' looks like the animal in the picture and means to carry or endure, the sense in 'bear the cost'. 'Permanently dirty' is a verb, not an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: bear -> SUSTAIN: to bear a weight, a cost or a loss is to sustain it, the verb of holding up under strain.

clue.text: Spanish point out Tenerife is crap

indicators.note: Out here means out of order rather than spoken aloud, and letters out of order have to be settled into a new arrangement.

parts.note: anagram fodder, fourteen letters

explanation.surface: Spaniards declaring that the holiday island of Tenerife is rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Point out' reads as one phrase, which is the trap: the definition stops after 'point' and 'out' does the shuffling. The name of the headland means land's end.
explanation.definitionFit: Spanish point -> CAPE FINISTERRE: a cape is a point of land, and this one juts out from Galicia in north-west Spain.

clue.text: Weathercocks on English church vanish

indicators.note: A weathercock stands on top of what holds it, and in an across clue the thing stood on is written first, so its letter leads.

parts.note: E = English, the usual single letter for the language
a weathercock is a weather vane, so the plural supplies five letters
CE = Church of England, the established English church

explanation.surface: Weather vanes turning on the tower of an English parish church.
explanation.walkthrough: Across clues use 'on' the way a builder does: the piece written second is underneath, so a fragment sitting on something follows it rather than leading.
explanation.definitionFit: vanish -> EVANESCE: to evanesce is to fade from sight and dissipate, the literary verb for vanishing by degrees.

clue.text: Sent after the French in retreat

definitions.note: 'Sent' is a past participle where the answer is an adjective; the setter means it in the sense 'sent by post', which is what the adjective describes.

indicators.note: An army in retreat goes back the way it came, so the French word's letters are written in the opposite order along this across entry.

parts.note: post means after, as in post-war or post-match
the French for 'the' is la, here written backwards

explanation.surface: Somebody sent in pursuit of the French as they fall back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The French' is crossword shorthand for the French word for 'the' — LE, LA or LES — and the surface is banking on you picturing actual Frenchmen.
explanation.definitionFit: Sent -> POSTAL: a postal vote or postal order is one sent through the post, which is the sense 'sent' is pointing at.

clue.text: Large area breakdown service covers remains subject to review

indicators.note: To cover a thing is to lie over it from both sides, so the service's two letters part and take the rest between them.
A review goes back over what has been done, and letters gone back over come out in the opposite order.

parts.note: the AA is the Automobile Association, the British motoring club that rescues broken-down cars
what remains still is, and those two letters are turned round

explanation.surface: An insurance question: whether the roadside rescue policy covers wreckage still under investigation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Covers' does two jobs at once — insurance cover in the picture, enclosure in the wordplay — and 'remains' is the verb, not the noun for what is left behind.
explanation.definitionFit: Large area -> ASIA: the biggest of the continents, so the definition points at it by size and kind rather than by synonym.

clue.text: Spooner's someone who played Cowboys and Indians for mental activity

definitions.note: The answer is plural and 'mental activity' a mass noun; the electrical traffic in a head is always counted in the plural, so the mass noun covers it.

indicators.note: The Reverend Spooner's trademark slip traded the opening sounds of two words, so say the phrase aloud and swap the noises at the front.

parts.note: John Wayne spent a career in the saddle, and his name said aloud hands its opening sound to the other word
braves are Indian warriors, and this word passes its opening sound forward in the exchange

explanation.surface: Remembering somebody who used to play Cowboys and Indians in the back garden.
explanation.walkthrough: John Wayne made his name in westerns and 'braves' is the old word for Indian warriors, so the children's game hides two very different things. Only the noises at the front move; the vowels stay where they are.
explanation.definitionFit: mental activity -> BRAINWAVES: the rhythms an EEG traces are the brain's electrical activity, and the singular also means a bright idea.

clue.text: Butchered head on stick

indicators.note: A butcher cuts a carcass into pieces and puts none of it back as it was, so the letters that follow come apart and reassemble in another order.

parts.note: the four letters of HEAD, cut up and relaid
re means on, as in 're your letter' — on the subject of

explanation.surface: A butchered head mounted on the end of a pole.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' is the small trap: it reads as joinery saying where the head goes, and it is a piece of the answer in its own right, since re means on in the sense of concerning.
explanation.definitionFit: stick -> ADHERE: to adhere is to stick fast to a surface, and figuratively to stick to a rule or a plan.

clue.text: Blithe director switched live broadcast

indicators.note: Switched means turned about, so the two letters it applies to change places and are written the other way round.

parts.note: D = director, as on a company letterhead
to live is to be, and those two letters are written the other way round
a programme being broadcast is on air

explanation.surface: A carefree director changing the live broadcast at the last minute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Live broadcast' looks like one phrase and is two separate pieces of wordplay, while 'Blithe' defines from the very front, where a solver expects the wordplay to begin.
explanation.definitionFit: Blithe -> DEBONAIR: both name an easy, carefree cheerfulness, with debonair adding a suggestion of style along with it.

clue.text: Missile German shot with shocking noise overhead

indicators.note: Something shot to pieces has its parts scattered, so the six letters beside this word are re-laid in a new order.
Overhead means above, and in a down entry what is above is written first, so the noise takes the top cells.

parts.note: the noise you make to startle somebody is boo
the six letters of GERMAN scattered into a different order

explanation.surface: A German rocket coming over with a terrifying bang above the rooftops.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Missile' is fair for anything thrown at a target, not just a rocket, which is what the wartime surface wants you to picture instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Missile -> BOOMERANG: a missile is any object hurled as a weapon, and this is the throwing stick that returns to the thrower.

clue.text: That woman caught casing supermarket dealing in arms

definitions.note: 'Dealing in arms' is a participial phrase where the answer is an adjective; heraldry is the trade that deals in coats of arms, so the phrase describes what the adjective covers.

indicators.note: A case goes right round its contents, so the letters before this word open up and the supermarket sits inside them.

parts.note: 'that woman' as an object is her
Aldi is the German discount chain found on most British high streets
c = caught, from cricket scorecards where a batsman is caught out

explanation.surface: A woman arrested while scoping out a supermarket that sells weapons.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arms' is the pivot — guns in the picture, coats of arms in the definition — and 'casing' is thieves' slang for scouting a place, which is why the enclosure hides so well.
explanation.definitionFit: dealing in arms -> HERALDIC: heraldry is the design and study of coats of arms, so anything heraldic deals in arms of that kind.

clue.text: Where old fighter might roll up?

definitions.text: Where old fighter might roll up?

parts.note: the surface offers a veteran boxer, while the setter means a vintage aircraft
rolling up is what a latecomer does on the surface, and what a display pilot does in the air

explanation.surface: An old prizefighter ambling in late to some gathering.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no wordplay to separate out here: 'fighter' is the aeroplane rather than the boxer, and the roll is an aerobatic manoeuvre rather than an arrival.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue defines by picture: an air show is precisely where a vintage fighter turns up and performs rolls.

clue.text: American filling punch with vermouth turned red

indicators.note: Turned means turned over, so the vermouth's two letters come out the other way up in this down entry.
A filling goes into the middle of whatever it fills, so the American letter drops inside the punch.

parts.note: to punch someone is to chin them, and these four letters part after the third
A = American, the single-letter shorthand
Italian vermouth is IT, from the bar order 'gin and It', written here the other way up

explanation.surface: An American mixing fruit punch with vermouth until the drink goes red.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Punch' is a drink in the picture and a blow in the wordplay, and IT for Italian vermouth is worth keeping — it comes from the old bar call 'gin and It'.
explanation.definitionFit: red -> CHIANTI: a red is a red wine, and Chianti is the Tuscan one, so the definition names it by example.

clue.text: Ugly beast concealed natural beauty

parts.note: an orc is the ugly brute of Tolkien's stories, a standard crossword monster
concealed is the past tense of hide

explanation.surface: A monster lurking somewhere lovely and unspoilt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Concealed' looks like the signal for a hidden word, so the temptation is to comb the clue's letters for something buried; here it is simply a chunk of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: natural beauty -> ORCHID: a flower prized for its looks, so the definition points at a thing of natural beauty rather than at scenery.

clue.text: Charles with Anne as his relation in carriage

parts.note: Chas is the everyday short form of Charles
Princess Anne is Charles's sister, and sis is the familiar short form

explanation.surface: Charles introducing Anne as his sister while the two of them ride in a carriage.
explanation.walkthrough: The royal siblings are real, which is what makes the picture hold together, and the clue banks on 'carriage' being the thing they are sitting in rather than the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: carriage -> CHASSIS: the chassis is the frame a vehicle's body rests on, and carriage is used of that load-bearing under-frame.

clue.text: Support for writer really bored by criticism in Ireland

indicators.note: To bore into a thing is to drill through its middle, so the word being bored opens and takes the borer inside it.

parts.note: Eire is the Irish name for the Republic of Ireland, and these letters split after the first

indicators.note: In puts one set of letters within another, so everything assembled so far sits inside the country's name.

parts.note: really means so, as in 'so very tired', and the two letters part
a crit is a piece of criticism, the art-school short form

explanation.surface: Backing for an author who is thoroughly bored by the reviews coming out of Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Support' sounds like moral backing and means furniture, and 'bored' is the drilling sense rather than the yawning one the surface offers.
explanation.definitionFit: Support for writer -> ESCRITOIRE: an escritoire is a writing desk, the piece of furniture that holds a writer's work up.

clue.text: Root vegetables out of Northern Ireland could be thinner

indicators.note: Out of takes the second thing away from the first, so those two letters walk out of the vegetables and leave the rest.

parts.note: turnips are the root vegetables, seven letters to start from
NI is the standard abbreviation for Northern Ireland, and those two letters sit together in the middle of the vegetables

explanation.surface: Root vegetables grown outside Northern Ireland turning out on the scrawny side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thinner' is a noun, not a comparative adjective: the stuff painters use to thin oil paint. Turps is short for turpentine and does exactly that job.
explanation.definitionFit: thinner -> TURPS: turpentine is the solvent painters use to thin paint, so 'thinner' names the product by what it does.

clue.text: Voice instruction to open Format menu?

parts.note: the Alt key is the modifier that begins a keyboard command
Alt plus a menu's underlined letter opens it, and the letter picked out of Format is its second

explanation.surface: A prompt telling you which keys will open the Format menu on screen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Voice' defines from the front, where the wordplay usually starts. On a Windows menu bar Format's shortcut uses its second letter, because File has already claimed the F.
explanation.definitionFit: Voice -> ALTO: alto is the singing voice between soprano and tenor, so the definition names the answer by its category.

clue.text: Rats black and not black, presumably

parts.note: b = black, as on a pencil and in chess notation
anything that is not the colour named is of some other colour, and 'presumably' admits that is an assumption

explanation.surface: A note on a survey form: some of the rats were black and the rest, presumably, were not.
explanation.walkthrough: Definition and answer are both mild oaths, which is the hard part — exclamations are easy to forget have synonyms — and 'Rats' looks like the animals the rest of the clue counts.
explanation.definitionFit: Rats -> BOTHER: both are mild exclamations of annoyance, interchangeable in 'Oh, rats!' and 'Oh, bother!'

clue.text: Flipping reckless cutting new tree for DIY project after storm warning

indicators.note: Flipping a thing turns it over, so the reckless letters go in back to front; it doubles as the mild swear the surface wants.

parts.note: n = new, the standard single letter

indicators.note: Cutting into something opens a gap and the cutter sits in it, so the turned letters land inside the tree.

parts.note: the oak is the tree, and its three letters part before the last
reckless is rash, and those four letters are written back to front

explanation.surface: An exasperated home builder hacking into a new tree to get something finished before the storm arrives.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a joke rather than a synonym: the ark was the original home build, started once its owner had the flood forecast. 'Flipping' reads as exasperation and works as the turn.
explanation.definitionFit: DIY project after storm warning -> NOAH'S ARK: Noah built the boat himself once he had been warned the flood was coming.

clue.text: Is no more fuel in can confirmed? It's a non-renewable resource

indicators.note: In drops one piece inside another, so the fuel is written between the can and the word meaning confirmed.

parts.note: whatever is no more once was, so the past tense of 'is' supplies three letters
a can is a tin
gas is fuel, and in America the fuel that goes in a car
a date or a plan that is confirmed is set

explanation.surface: Checking whether the last of the fuel in the can has really run out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is no more' looks like the euphemism for dead and is doing plain grammar — the past tense of 'is' — and the definition is the whole closing phrase, not just its final word.
explanation.definitionFit: a non-renewable resource -> WASTING ASSET: in accounting a wasting asset is one used up and never replaced, which is what such a resource is.
